rationale: A wins because it breaks the update into separate reporter questions with separate protagonists: “Whatnot won't say how much of its $3B in sales actually reaches sellers” is a real story, not a company victory lap. B has sharper proof discipline, but “Whatnot is betting US shoppers behave like Asia's — the data so far says they don't” spends data the fact block did not give it. A gives the founder more pitchable lanes with fewer invented supports.
gaps_in_A: “Does Whatnot's math hold up: $3B in sales, a near-$5B price tag, and a take rate nobody's seen” leans on a stale valuation without proving there is a current financing or investor-news peg.

“Whatnot bets its trading-card crowd will also buy sneakers and laptops” implies the same buyer base will migrate; the update says new categories, not that existing collectors are the audience for them.
“Whatnot is betting the US will finally shop the way Asia already does” is directionally grounded, but still needs a cited Asia-vs-US benchmark before it can carry a trend pitch.
gaps_in_B: “US-born platform” is not in the update. Small phrase, real problem: invented background detail is how sloppy drafts start lying politely.
“the data so far says they don't” is the biggest foul. The update says Asia is larger; it does not supply data proving US shoppers reject the behavior.
“long-running, repeatedly-failed attempts to make Western live shopping work” may be true in the real world, but it is not in the provided facts and cannot be asserted in this blind exercise.
“The reporter can use $3B as the first hard data point that the format scales past collectors” overclaims. Without a category split, the $3B could still be mostly collectibles.
